questions.question: Additional comments:
How relevant did you find your traineeship for your future employment prospects? *
questions.answer:
This traineeship played an important role in shaping how I now envision my professional future. Through my daily research tasks, I gained a much clearer understanding of what academic research looks like in practice and what it requires on a sustained, everyday level.

This experience confirmed my intention to pursue a PhD! :)  Engaging closely with research design, data work, and academic writing, particularly through my contribution to the Safe Country of Origin database and the drafting of a working paper (I have also published for the first time in my life - a policy brief)  allowed me to see myself more clearly in a research role. I felt super confident that the skills I developed during this traineeship provide a solid foundation for my future PhD. 

Beyond this academic confirmation, the traineeship also helped me realise that I had, at least for this stage of my life, found the kind of environment in which I would like to work and grow. Being part of a university-based research centre, embedded in an interdisciplinary and international academic community, gave me a strong sense of professional belonging. The combination of research, intellectual exchange, and institutional engagement resonated with my aspirations.

Overall, this experience did not simply contribute to my skill development, but also offered clarity and reassurance regarding my future direction. It strengthened my motivation to continue along an academic path and to build a long-term career in research, ideally within similar institutional settings.

questions.question: How relevant did you find your traineeship for your academic programme at UCPH *
questions.answer:
I found the traineeship highly relevant for my academic programme (Advanced Migration Studies) at the KU. The experience allowed me to apply and critically reflect on many of the theoretical concepts and methodological approaches I had learned during my first MA's year, particularly in relation to asylum governance, migration management, and the production of legal and administrative categories.

Through my work at the Centre for Migration, Diversity and Justice, I was able to translate abstract concepts from the programme (such as bordering practices, categorisation, and the relationship between law, policy, and power) into concrete research tasks. In particular, my involvement in the construction of the Safe Country of Origin database provided a practical lens through which to understand how migration governance operates through seemingly technical classifications. This directly resonated with core discussions in the Advanced Migration Studies programme on state practices, discretion, and institutionalised forms of exclusion.

Methodologically, the traineeship complemented the programme’s strong emphasis on qualitative research. Conducting data coding, and preliminary analysis helped me deepen my methodological skills and reflect more critically on questions of positionality, interpretation, and research ethics (issues that are central to the academic training at UCPH).

More broadly, the traineeship functioned as an extension of my academic learning rather than a parallel or separate experience. It strengthened my ability to connect theory and empirical research, clarified how academic knowledge is produced beyond the classroom, and supported my ongoing thesis work. As such, I experienced the traineeship not only as relevant, but as integral to my development within the Advanced Migration Studies programme.

questions.question: Additional comments
How well did the academic level at UCPH coincide with the tasks completed during your traineeship? *
questions.answer: I'd say very well :)

questions.question: Please elaborate *
questions.answer:
1. The programme’s strong theoretical and methodological foundation: I felt super prepared to engage meaningfully with the research activities at the Centre for Migration, Diversity and Justice, rather than merely performing technical or administrative tasks.

2. The analytical frameworks and critical perspectives developed during my studies enabled me to approach tasks such as policy classification, and database construction with an informed and reflective mindset. In particular, the programme’s emphasis on critical migration studies allowed me to recognise the political and normative dimensions embedded in legal and administrative categories, including those underlying Safe Country of Origin policies.

3. The qualitative research training at UCPH (specially in the course "Migration and Socities", where we needed to conduct a fieldwork study) corresponded with the tasks I carried out during the traineeship. Skills acquired through coursework, such as critical reading, data interpretation, and reflexive analysis, were directly applicable to p.eg the construction and the reflection of the SCO Database. 

Overall, the academic level at UCPH did not merely coincide with the traineeship tasks, but actively enabled me to perform them with confidence and analytical depth. The traineeship thus served as a practical extension of my academic training, reinforcing the relevance and applicability of the Advanced Migration Studies programme.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your traineeship destination (city/region)? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available at your traineeship destination (organization/city/region)? *
questions.answer:
During my stay in Brussels, the city offered a rich professional and cultural environment that complemented my traineeship experience. In addition to numerous conferences and events related to the work of the European Parliament and the topic of Migration (such as events organised by The Left on the issue of deportation, and the establishment of the SCO EU list, or a memorandum organised by the Spanish Political Groups of the Parliament for the victims of Franco), I benefited from the broader cultural life of the city:

In particular, the EUROPALIA festival coincided with my stay, and the fact that Spain was the country of focus that year allowed me to engage with cultural expressions closely connected to my own background. Attending flamenco performances, theatre productions, and art exhibitions fostered a sense of familiarity and belonging, which positively contributed to my overall integration and well-being during the traineeship.

Furthermore, the VUB had a swimming pool where members could get discounts. And once again, I was lucky enough to live very close to La Chambre, a beautiful park in the city of Brussels where I went running quite often.

questions.question: Which non-academic activities would you recommend to future trainees visiting the same destination (organization/city/region)? Why? *
questions.answer:
attending cultural festivals, food markets, thrift shops, exhibitions and performing arts events, such as theatre and music concerts. I also love Belgian beers, which are exceptional and unique (if I can say). Museums are also great, or they could just disconnect and walk through the streets of Brussels or sit in a nice square and have a coffee in a bakery (Renard, where the best Cream Croissants ever!). They could even go to their neighbourhood city forum in the neighbourhood parliament, if they speak French. 

I would also recommend attending public talks, debates, and exhibitions hosted by EU institutions, cultural centres, or civil society organisations. These events often bridge political, and cultural perspectives and allow trainees to engage with topics related to European governance and migration in a more informal setting.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting trainees see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore Belgium! I went to Ghent, Bruges and Antwerp, for instance, and they were all super beautiful cities with a good train system from Brussels (tains run every 20 minutes & until quite late at night)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your trainee host? *
questions.answer: It's very easy, and they also organise lots of social events. One day, we did a line dance!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of the destination (city/country)? *
questions.answer: It was actually super easy. I'd say that life in Brussels is very similar to life in Spain – at least in the area where I was living, which was always super crowded and busy, even during the week. And for a central European country, the weather wasn't that bad. At the same time, I loved the multicultural character of the city and the fact that wherever I went, I could hear Spanish speakers.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with locals? *
questions.answer: I met my "best friend" in the city through the Facebook Marketplace, where I bought a sofa from her. So I'd say this could be a nice way to meet people, as well as attending to the city forums.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I'd say that places (local shos) are closing at 6 pm and also supermarkets at 8.00 pm

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I'd say the area I lived in - Flagey. But also the surroundings of my office (the VUB campus), Fernand Coq Square and La Chambre.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going on a traineeship to the same city/region? *
questions.answer:
1. The city is very car-friendly, so if they are planning to cycle, they need to be very careful. The city is not very suitable for cyclists (bad bike lanes - sometimes the bike lane is where the tram is going..). It's not even close to Dutch standards. Bikes can also get stolen very easily :( 
2. Take a proactive approach to your internship. The project or task you want to work on will not just land in your lap; you need to actively ask and show interest in the activities so that people can trust you. 
3. The EU bubble in this city, consisting of traineeships and people working in EU institutions, is very real, and sometimes it can be a little intimidating.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future traineeship students? *
questions.answer:
1. Go to Troc, the best place to buy furniture (I bought four chairs for €40). 
2. Be careful when drinking beer as it has a high alcohol concentration... (sometimes one beer can have 11%)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your traineeship experience? *
questions.answer:
From an academic perspective: the opportunity to meaningfully contribute to ongoing academic research. Being entrusted with the construction of the Safe Country of Origin database and the contribution to a working paper made me feel just great. Also another big milestone was when my first policy brief was published. I felt super grateful for having the opportunity to work with Gaia Romeo, she was super nice to me and I learned a lot from her. 

I also found especially rewarding to see how abstract concepts discussed during my studies were translated into concrete research practices and policy-relevant outputs: engaging with legal and policy data across different national contexts deepened my understanding of how migration governance operates in practice and highlighted the importance critical research in this field.

On a personal level, I had the opportunity to live with my partner here in Brussels, where he was granted an EU-related internship at the same time I was granted with this traineeship position. This allowed us to be together in this city, as we are in a long-distance relationship. 

Overall, I was the happiest girl and I feel super grateful and blessed that I was given this opportunity.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the traineeship? *
questions.answer: I needed to work two jobs at the same time -  I kept my job in Copenhagen and the internship here, for financial reasons, which was very challenging as I had to work an extra two hours every day.

questions.question: Is there anything UCPH could have done different (before/during/after) in regard to the traineeship experience? *
questions.answer: Everything was great on the UCPH side -  I don't have any complaints. Special thanks to Shabnam for being so helpful and understanding throughout the process.
